newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels say government blocks talks progress.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels say government blocks talks progress.

text.p: Marxist rebels said on Saturday they were ready for direct talks with Peru's government, but its refusal to consider their demand to free jailed comrades was blocking negotiations to end the 32-day hostage crisis.

Within a framework of discussing all issues, including the demand to free some 400 jailed rebels, "we are ready to converse as we were willing to since we occupied this diplomatic site," said a Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) spokesman via two-way radio.

However, the government's refusal to consider their principal demand means "there is no possibility of starting conversations because in practice they are asking us beforehand to drop our request, which signifies a formal call to surrender which we will never accept," he added.
In a five-point communique, the MRTA accepted the government's proposal of a Canadian government representative on a "guarantor" committee overseeing the talks.

"The government proposal to include a representative from Canada is acceptable," said the spokesman, assumed to be MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini speaking from within the besieged Japanese ambassador's home.
Government negotiator Domingo Palermo said on Friday former hostage and Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent would sit on the commission. But he ruled out considering the release of MRTA prisoners.

The Japanese government's task force in Lima cautiously welcomed the MRTA communique as at least focusing the precise point of dispute and recognising the need for private rather than public negotiations. "The distance is becoming smaller," a task force official said.
Hours later, police evicted six journalists from the roof of a building near the besieged residence.

Five photographers and a television cameraman, mostly from international news agencies, were ordered down from the vantage point they had manned in shifts, hauling up food by rope, for the 32 days since the siege began.
The order was signed by police Gen. Fernando Gamero Febres and obliged the journalists to come down "for strict reasons of security". The eviction took place without incident.
Hundreds more journalists are camped out in the environs of the besieged residence, behind police cordons placed at a distance of two city blocks on all four sides.

Shortly before the eviction, an explosion disrupted the relative calm around the residence, where more than 500 hostages were originally taken during a Dec. 17 party to celebrate the Japanese Emperor's birthday.
Local media speculated the blast was caused by a guerrilla car bomb, but police officials later said the noise came from a shootout with three criminals, unrelated to the siege.

The rebels inside the booby-trapped and mined compound in Lima also launched a fresh propaganda offensive on Saturday, unfurling three banners that struck comparisons between their hostages, Peru's poor and their jailed colleagues.

"Most of the population would like to feed themselves as well as the authorities held here," read one message, referring to the meals provided daily by the Red Cross during the 32-day siege. "These differences justify the people's struggle."

The rebels' banners blew over during the morning, but two hostages emerged on the roof on Saturday afternoon to rearrange them. They were identified by the task force as Japanese embassy attache Shinji Yamamoto and second secretary Akihisa Ougiyama.

The MRTA has held onto those men it considers the best bargaining chips, including top government and security force officials, dozens of Japanese businessmen and diplomats and the younger brother of Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori.
The government announced on Saturday the formation of a special support committee, consisting of eight mental health specialists, to help relatives of the hostages.
But authorities were forced to cancel plans to celebrate Saturday's 462nd anniversary of the founding of Lima out of respect for the hostages.

Roman Catholic bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, whom both sides have agreed will sit on the "guarantor" committee, entered the residence to spend several hours with the hostages on Saturday afternoon. He did not speak to reporters on his exit.
